claim: Memories are stored as ensembles of engram neurons and their successful recall involves the reactivation of these cellular networks.
source: Memories are stored as ensembles of engram neurons and their successful recall involves the reactivation of these cellular networks.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus in the field of memory research, supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: Mice tested 24 hr after training spent significantly more time exploring the novel object compared to the familiar object, t(9) = 5.12, p<0.001, 95% CI [11.18–28.68].
source: During object memory recall, mice tested 24 hr after training spent significantly more time exploring the novel object compared to the familiar object, t(9) = 5.12, p<0.001, 95% CI [11.18–28.68].
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data showing significant difference in exploration time.

claim: Mice tested 2 weeks after training spent a similar amount of time exploring both novel and familiar objects, t(11) = 0.93, p=0.36, 95% CI [–3.88 to 9.64].
source: Mice that were tested 2 weeks after training spent a similar amount of time exploring both novel and familiar objects, t(11) = 0.93, p=0.36, 95% CI [–3.88 to 9.64] (Figure 1b).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data showing no significant difference in exploration time, with reference to Figure 1b.

claim: There was a significant difference between the discrimination index of the 24 hr and 2 week group, t(20) = 4.30, p<0.001, 95% CI [–0.59 to –0.20].
source: There was a significant difference between the discrimination index of the 24 hr and 2 week group, t(20) = 4.30, p<0.001, 95% CI [–0.59 to –0.20] (Figure 1c).
evidence: Statistical comparison of discrimination indices between two time points, with reference to Figure 1c.

claim: Mice successfully recall an object memory 24 hr after acquisition, while at 2 weeks there was no preference for the novel object suggesting the original familiar object had been forgotten.
source: Together, these data indicate that mice successfully recall an object memory 24 hr after acquisition, while at 2 weeks there was no preference for the novel object suggesting the original familiar object had been forgotten.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental data showing memory recall at 24 hours and forgetting at 2 weeks.

claim: There was no significant difference in the number of engram cells between the 24 hr and 2 week tested groups (eYFP+), t(6) = 0.18, p=0.86, 95% CI [–2.24 to 2.60].
source: When comparing the engram ensemble between the two cohorts, we observed no significant difference in the number of engram cells between the 24 hr and 2 week tested groups (eYFP+), t(6) = 0.18, p=0.86, 95% CI [–2.24 to 2.60] (Figure 1j and k).
evidence: Statistical analysis of engram cell counts showing no significant difference between groups, with reference to Figure 1j and k.

claim: There was no significant difference in c-Fos activity within the dentate gyrus between the 24 hr tested or 2 week tested mice, t(6) = 0.84, p=0.42, 95% CI [–1.37 to 0.66].
source: Similarly, there was no significant difference in c-Fos activity within the dentate gyrus between the 24 hr tested or 2 week tested mice, t(6) = 0.84, p=0.42, 95% CI [–1.37 to 0.66] (Figure 1l).
evidence: Statistical analysis of c-Fos activity showing no significant difference between groups, with reference to Figure 1l.

claim: There was a significant decrease in engram reactivation in mice that were tested 2 weeks after training and that had forgotten the object memory, t(6) = 4.56, p=0.003, 95% CI [–14.96 to –4.52].
source: However, when comparing engram reactivation, i.e., the number of engram cells (eYFP+) that also expresses c-Fos during the recall test, which indicates these cells were active during encoding and then became active again during the memory recall (Figure 1j), there was a significant decrease in engram reactivation in mice that were tested 2 weeks after training and that had forgotten the object memory, t(6) = 4.56, p=0.003, 95% CI [–14.96 to –4.52] (Figure 1m).
evidence: Statistical analysis of engram reactivation showing significant decrease in the 2-week group, with reference to Figure 1j and 1m.

claim: The level of engram reactivation correlated with the performance in object discrimination, r(1, 6) = 0.61, p=0.02.
source: Furthermore, the level of engram reactivation correlated with the performance in object discrimination, r(1, 6) = 0.61, p=0.02 (Figure 1i).
evidence: Correlation analysis showing significant relationship between engram reactivation and discrimination performance, with reference to Figure 1i.

claim: Natural forgetting may be driven by a reduction in engram ensemble activity.
source: Together these data suggest that natural forgetting may be driven by a reduction in engram ensemble activity.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental findings showing correlation between reduced engram activity and forgetting.

claim: Following natural forgetting mice displayed a significant reduction in spine density, t(6) = 8.23, p<0.001, 95% CI [–4.55 to –2.46].
source: Following natural forgetting mice displayed a significant reduction in spine density, t(6) = 8.23, p<0.001, 95% CI [–4.55 to –2.46] (Figure 1n).
evidence: Statistical analysis of morphological data showing significant reduction in spine density, with reference to Figure 1n.

claim: There was a significant decrease in spine volume, t(372) = 4.50, p<0.001, 95% CI [–0.33 to –0.13].
source: Moreover, there was also a significant decrease in spine volume, t(372) = 4.50, p<0.001, 95% CI [–0.33 to –0.13] (Figure 1o and p).
evidence: Statistical analysis of morphological data showing significant decrease in spine volume, with reference to Figure 1o and p.

claim: In addition to the reduced engram activity, there was also a reduction in engram spine density following natural forgetting.
source: Together, these findings suggest that in addition to the reduced engram activity, there was also a reduction in engram spine density.
evidence: Summary of morphological findings showing structural changes in engrams after forgetting.

claim: No Light control mice spent significantly more time with the novel object compared to the familiar object, indicating successful memory retrieval, t(9) = 2.91, p=0.01, 95% CI [3.43–27.09].
source: During the object recall test the No Light control mice spent significantly more time with the novel object compared to the familiar object, indicating successful memory retrieval, t(9) = 2.91, p=0.01, 95% CI [3.43–27.09] (Figure 2b).
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data from control group showing successful memory retrieval, with reference to Figure 2b.

claim: Mice in which the engram was inhibited spent equal time exploring both the familiar and novel objects, indicating mice failed to distinguish the novel from the familiar object, t(8) = 0.58, p=0.57, 95% CI [–4.21 to 7.09].
source: Whereas mice in which the engram was inhibited spent equal time exploring both the familiar and novel objects, indicating mice failed to distinguish the novel from the familiar object, t(8) = 0.58, p=0.57, 95% CI [–4.21 to 7.09] (Figure 2b).
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data from optogenetic inhibition group showing impaired memory retrieval, with reference to Figure 2b.

claim: There was a significant difference between the discrimination index of the No Light control and Light-induced inhibition groups, t(17) = 2.18, p=0.04, 95% CI [–0.49 to –0.008].
source: There was a significant difference between the discrimination index of the No Light control and Light-induced inhibition groups, t(17) = 2.18, p=0.04, 95% CI [–0.49 to –0.008] (Figure 2c).
evidence: Statistical comparison of discrimination indices between control and inhibition groups, with reference to Figure 2c.

claim: The engram cells within the dentate gyrus are required for successful retrieval of an object memory.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that the engram cells within the dentate gyrus are required for successful retrieval of an object memory.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from optogenetic inhibition experiment showing necessity of engram cells for memory retrieval.

claim: No Light control mice displayed equal exploration of both the novel and familiar objects suggesting mice had forgotten the familiar object, t(10) = 1.81, p=0.10, 95% CI [–0.90 to 8.84].
source: During the object recall test the No Light control mice displayed equal exploration of both the novel and familiar objects suggesting mice had forgotten the familiar object, t(10) = 1.81, p=0.10, 95% CI [–0.90 to 8.84] (Figure 2e).
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data from control group showing forgetting, with reference to Figure 2e.

claim: Mice that underwent optogenetic activation spent more time exploring the novel object compared to the familiar object, suggesting the original object memory had been retrieved, t(7) = 3.41, p=0.01, 95% CI [3.71–20.43].
source: Whereas mice that underwent optogenetic activation spent more time exploring the novel object compared to the familiar object, suggesting the original object memory had been retrieved, t(7) = 3.41, p=0.01, 95% CI [3.71–20.43] (Figure 2e).
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data from optogenetic activation group showing memory retrieval, with reference to Figure 2e.

claim: There was a significant difference between the discrimination index of the No Light control and Light-induced activation group, t(17) = 2.14, p=0.04, 95% CI [0.002–0.34].
source: There was a significant difference between the discrimination index of the No Light control and Light-induced activation group, t(17) = 2.14, p=0.04, 95% CI [0.002–0.34] (Figure 2f).
evidence: Statistical comparison of discrimination indices between control and activation groups, with reference to Figure 2f.

claim: Artificial activation of the original engram was sufficient to induce recall of the forgotten object memory, and the forgotten engram was still intact.
source: These data suggest that artificial activation of the original engram was sufficient to induce recall of the forgotten object memory, and that the forgotten engram was still intact, otherwise activation of those cells would no longer trigger memory recall.
evidence: Interpretation of optogenetic activation results showing sufficiency of engram activation for memory retrieval and persistence of engram structure.

claim: Engram activity can modulate memory retrieval, where activation of the engram ensemble is both necessary for successful memory retrieval and sufficient to induce recall despite natural forgetting.
source: Together, the results of Figure 2 suggest that engram activity can modulate memory retrieval, where activation of the engram ensemble is both necessary for successful memory retrieval and sufficient to induce recall despite natural forgetting.
evidence: Summary conclusion from optogenetic experiments demonstrating necessity and sufficiency of engram activity for memory retrieval.

claim: Environmental enrichment has been shown to enhance cognitive function and improve memory retention.
source: Environmental enrichment has been shown to enhance cognitive function and improve memory retention (Bekinschtein et al., 2011; Gubert and Hannan, 2019; Clemenson et al., 2015; O'Leary et al., 2019a; O'Leary et al., 2019b).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: There was a significant effect of enriched housing on object memory performance F(3, 53)=3.26, p=0.028, 95% CI [–0.18 to 0.01].
source: There was a significant effect of enriched housing on object memory performance F(3, 53)=3.26, p=0.028, 95% CI [–0.18 to 0.01] (Figure 3b).
evidence: Statistical analysis showing significant effect of enrichment on memory performance, with reference to Figure 3b.

claim: There was no difference in object memory performance between the standard housed (Std) or environmental enrichment housed (EE) mice when tested 24 hr or 1 week after acquisition training, indicating no change in memory recall.
source: Bonferroni post hoc comparisons indicated there was no difference in object memory performance between the standard housed (Std) or environmental enrichment housed (EE) mice when tested 24 hr or 1 week after acquisition training, indicating no change in memory recall (Figure 3b).
evidence: Post hoc statistical analysis showing no difference at early time points, with reference to Figure 3b.

claim: There was a significant difference in discrimination index between standard housed and enriched mice when tested 2 hr after training (p=0.047), suggesting the enriched housed mice were still able to recall the familiar object, whereas the standard housed mice had forgotten.
source: However, there was a significant difference in discrimination index between standard housed and enriched mice when tested 2 hr after training (p=0.047), suggesting the enriched housed mice were still able to recall the familiar object, whereas the standard housed mice had forgotten.
evidence: Post hoc statistical analysis showing significant difference at 2 weeks, indicating differential forgetting rates.

claim: Mice housed in enrichment maintained the object memory 2 weeks after training, as they spent more time exploring the novel object compared to the familiar object, t(11) = 5.05, p<0.001, 95% CI [8.59–21.83].
source: Again, we observed that mice housed in enrichment maintained the object memory 2 weeks after training, as they spent more time exploring the novel object compared to the familiar object, t(11) = 5.05, p<0.001, 95% CI [8.59–21.83].
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data from enriched mice showing maintained memory at 2 weeks.

claim: Mice housed in standard housing spent a similar amount of time exploring both the novel and familiar objects, t(11)=1.77, p=0.10, 95% CI [–1.34 to 12.57].
source: Mice housed in standard housing spent a similar amount of time exploring both the novel and familiar objects, t(11)=1.77, p=0.10, 95% CI [–1.34 to 12.57] (Figure 3c).
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data from standard housed mice showing forgetting, with reference to Figure 3c.

claim: There was a significant difference between the discrimination index of standard housed (Std) and enriched (EE) mice, t(22) = 2.75, p=0.01, 95 % CI [0.054–0.38].
source: There was a significant difference between the discrimination index of standard housed (Std) and enriched (EE) mice, t(22) = 2.75, p=0.01, 95 % CI [0.054–0.38] (Figure 3d).
evidence: Statistical comparison of discrimination indices between housing conditions, with reference to Figure 3d.

claim: There was no significant difference in the number of engram cells following enrichment, t(12) = 0.56, p=0.58, 95% CI [–3.09 to 1.82].
source: When comparing the engram size between standard and enriched mice, we observed no significant difference in the number of engram cells following enrichment, t(12) = 0.56, p=0.58, 95% CI [–3.09 to 1.82] (Figure 3e and f).
evidence: Statistical analysis of engram cell counts showing no difference between housing conditions, with reference to Figure 3e and f.

claim: There was no significant difference in c-Fos activity, t(12) = 1.45, p=0.17, 95% CI [–0.62 to 3.13].
source: Similarly, there was also no significant difference in c-Fos activity, t(12) = 1.45, p=0.17, 95% CI [–0.62 to 3.13] (Figure 3g).
evidence: Statistical analysis of c-Fos activity showing no difference between housing conditions, with reference to Figure 3g.

claim: There was a significant increase in engram reactivation in mice that underwent enrichment, t(12) = 3.52, p=0.004, 95% CI [2.84–12.06].
source: However, there was a significant increase in engram reactivation in mice that underwent enrichment, t(12) = 3.52, p=0.004, 95% CI [2.84–12.06] (Figure 3h).
evidence: Statistical analysis showing significant increase in engram reactivation with enrichment, with reference to Figure 3h.

claim: Environmental enrichment reduces the rate of forgetting, by increasing or maintaining engram reactivation.
source: These data suggest that environmental enrichment reduces the rate of forgetting, by increasing or maintaining engram reactivation.
evidence: Interpretation of enrichment experiment results showing relationship between enrichment, engram reactivation, and forgetting.

claim: Enrichment increased hippocampal neurogenesis, with both the number of immature neurons (doublecortin+ cells) and neuronal survival (BrdU-NeuN-positive cells).
source: Enrichment increased hippocampal neurogenesis, with both the number of immature neurons (doublecortin+ cells) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and neuronal survival (BrdU-NeuN-positive cells) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Experimental data showing increased neurogenesis markers with enrichment, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: A brief exposure to reminder cues can aid memory recall.
source: Previous work from both human experimental psychology studies and rodent behavioral paradigms have shown that a brief exposure to reminder cues can aid memory recall (Wahlheim et al., 2019; Tambini et al., 2017; Finkelstein et al., 2022; Bouton, 1993).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research in humans and rodents.

claim: Mice given only a brief acquisition period of 5 min exhibited no preference for the novel object when tested 1 hr after training, suggesting the absence of a lasting object memory.
source: Mice given only a brief acquisition period of 5 min exhibited no preference for the novel object when tested 1 hr after training, suggesting the absence of a lasting object memory (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Control experiment data showing insufficient learning with brief acquisition, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Control group mice spent a similar amount of time exploring both the novel and familiar object, t(10) = 1.62, p=0.13, 95% CI [–1.13 to 7.22], suggesting the original object memory was forgotten.
source: During the object recall test, mice within the control group spent a similar amount of time exploring both the novel and familiar object, t(10) = 1.62, p=0.13, 95% CI [–1.13 to 7.22], again suggesting the original object memory was forgotten (Figure 4b).
evidence: Statistical analysis of control group showing forgetting, with reference to Figure 4b.

claim: Mice given a brief reminder session 1 hr prior to the recall test spent significantly more time exploring the novel object compared to the familiar object, t(4) = 4.63, p<0.01, 95% CI [7.27–29.00].
source: However, mice given a brief reminder session 1 hr prior to the recall test spent significantly more time exploring the novel object compared to the familiar object, t(4) = 4.63, p<0.01, 95% CI [7.27–29.00] (Figure 4b).
evidence: Statistical analysis of reminder group showing memory retrieval, with reference to Figure 4b.

claim: There was a significant difference between the discrimination index of the control and reminder group, t(14) = 4.57, p=0.001, 95% CI [0.19–0.54].
source: There was a significant difference between the discrimination index of the control and reminder group, t(14) = 4.57, p=0.001, 95% CI [0.19–0.54] (Figure 4c).
evidence: Statistical comparison of discrimination indices between control and reminder groups, with reference to Figure 4c.

claim: The mice that underwent the reminder session and displayed intact memory recall also exhibited an increase in original engram reactivation, t(8) = 3.13, p=0.014, 95% CI [2.66–17.57].
source: Furthermore, the mice that underwent the reminder session and displayed intact memory recall also exhibited an increase in original engram reactivation, t(8) = 3.13, p=0.014, 95% CI [2.66–17.57] (Figure 4d and g)
evidence: Statistical analysis showing increased engram reactivation with reminder, with reference to Figure 4d and g.

claim: There was no difference in the engram size, t(8) = 0.14, p=0.88, 95% CI [–1.76 to 1.55].
source: while there was no difference in the engram size, t(8) = 0.14, p=0.88, 95% CI [–1.76 to 1.55] (Figure 4e)
evidence: Statistical analysis showing no difference in engram size with reminder, with reference to Figure 4e.

claim: There was no difference in the level of neuronal activity within the dentate gyrus, t(8) = 0.11, p=0.91, 95% CI [–1.16 to 1.05].
source: or the level of neuronal activity within the dentate gyrus, t(8) = 0.11, p=0.91, 95% CI [–1.16 to 1.05] (Figure 4f).
evidence: Statistical analysis showing no difference in overall neuronal activity with reminder, with reference to Figure 4f.

claim: Repeated reminder trials spaced over several days was sufficient to facilitate persistent object memory recall.
source: The results indicated that repeated reminder trials spaced over several days was also sufficient to facilitate persistent object memory recall (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Experimental results showing effect of repeated reminders on memory, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: A brief reminder or subsequent object reminders over time facilitates the transition of a forgotten memory to an accessible memory via modulating engram activity.
source: Together, these data indicate that a brief reminder or subsequent object reminders over time facilitates the transition of a forgotten memory to an accessible memory via modulating engram activity.
evidence: Summary conclusion from reminder experiments showing mechanism of memory retrieval through engram modulation.

claim: Control mice spent significantly more time exploring the novel object compared to the familiar object, indicating a retrievable object memory, t(7) = 4.14, p=0.004, 95% CI [5.45–19.92].
source: During the recall test 1 week after training control mice spent significantly more time exploring the novel object compared to the familiar object, indicating a retrievable object memory, t(7) = 4.14, p=0.004, 95% CI [5.45–19.92] (Figure 5b).
evidence: Statistical analysis of control group showing intact memory at 1 week, with reference to Figure 5b.

claim: Mice that had been repeatedly exposed to the training environment devoid of objects spent a similar amount of time exploring both the novel and familiar objects, t(8) = 1.26, p=0.24, 95% CI [–5.29 to 18.18], suggesting an updated and now inaccessible engram.
source: Whereas mice that had been repeatedly exposed to the training environment devoid of objects spent a similar amount of time exploring both the novel and familiar objects, t(8) = 1.26, p=0.24, 95% CI [–5.29 to 18.18], suggesting an updated and now inaccessible engram.
evidence: Statistical analysis of context-only exposure group showing accelerated forgetting.

claim: There was a significant difference in the discrimination index between the control and empty box exposed mice, t(15) = 2.83, p=0.012, 95% CI [–0.55 to –0.077].
source: There was a significant difference in the discrimination index between the control and empty box exposed mice, t(15) = 2.83, p=0.012, 95% CI [–0.55 to –0.077] (Figure 5c).
evidence: Statistical comparison of discrimination indices between control and context-only groups, with reference to Figure 5c.

claim: Context-only mice showed increased object exploration, F(3, 30)=11.30, p=0.005.
source: Indeed, cross-groups comparison reveals mice in the context-only group showed increased object exploration, F(3, 30)=11.30, p=0.005.
evidence: Statistical analysis showing increased exploration in context-only group.

claim: Context-only mice explore the novel object (p=0.028) and object familiar (p=0.001) more than control mice.
source: A post hoc Tukey test showed that context-only mice explore the novel object, p=0.028, and object familiar, p=0.001 more than control mice.
evidence: Post hoc statistical analysis showing increased exploration of both objects in context-only group.

claim: No Light control group spent a similar amount of time exploring both the novel and familiar objects, t(9) = 1.36, p=0.20, 95% CI [–2.04 to 8.27].
source: During the recall test, the No Light control group spent a similar amount of time exploring both the novel and familiar objects, t(9) = 1.36, p=0.20, 95% CI [–2.04 to 8.27] (Figure 5e)
evidence: Statistical analysis of no light control group showing forgetting, with reference to Figure 5e.

claim: Light-induced inhibition mice, in which the engram was silenced, spent significantly more time exploring the novel object compared to the familiar object, t(11) = 3.60, p=0.004, 95% CI [4.70–19.46].
source: while the Light-induced inhibition mice, in which the engram was silenced, spent significantly more time exploring the novel object compared to the familiar object, t(11) = 3.60, p=0.004, 95% CI [4.70–19.46] (Figure 5e).
evidence: Statistical analysis of optogenetic inhibition group showing preserved memory, with reference to Figure 5e.

claim: There was a significant difference in discrimination index between No Light control and Light-induced inhibition group, t(20) = 2.12, p=0.046, 95% CI [0.003–0.33].
source: There was a significant difference in discrimination index between No Light control and Light-induced inhibition group, t(20) = 2.12, p=0.046, 95% CI [0.003–0.33] (Figure 5f).
evidence: Statistical comparison of discrimination indices between control and inhibition groups, with reference to Figure 5f.

claim: Experience following the encoding of an object memory can update the original memory engram accelerating the rate at which the information is forgotten, and this adaptive process requires the activity of the original engram ensemble.
source: Combined these data suggest that experience following the encoding of an object memory can update the original memory engram accelerating the rate at which the information is forgotten. Further, this adaptive process requires the activity of the original engram ensemble.
evidence: Summary conclusion from context-only exposure and optogenetic inhibition experiments showing experience-dependent forgetting requires engram activity.

claim: Rac1 has previously been shown to be involved in memory encoding and consolidation as well as active forgetting of contextual and social memory.
source: Rac1 has previously been shown to be involved in memory encoding and consolidation as well as active forgetting of contextual and social memory (Davis and Zhong, 2017; Liu et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2016; Shuai et al., 2010; Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2020; Berry et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to previous research on Rac1.

claim: Rac1 has also recently been shown to be involved in memory retrieval.
source: Rac1 has also recently been shown to be involved in memory retrieval (Lei et al., 2022).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to recent research.

claim: Mice that were administered saline displayed typical forgetting at 2 weeks, as indicated by similar object exploration between the novel and familiar objects, t(8) = 1.07, p=0.31, 95% CI [–2.61 to 7.20].
source: Mice that were administered saline displayed typical forgetting at 2 weeks, as indicated by similar object exploration between the novel and familiar objects, t(8) = 1.07, p=0.31, 95% CI [–2.61 to 7.20] (Figure 6b)
evidence: Statistical analysis of saline control group showing forgetting, with reference to Figure 6b.

claim: Mice treated with a Rac1 inhibitor displayed intact memory recall, spending significantly more time with the novel object compared to the familiar object, t(8) = 4.27, p=0.002, 95% CI [8.10–27.10].
source: while mice treated with a Rac1 inhibitor displayed intact memory recall, spending significantly more time with the novel object compared to the familiar object, t(8) = 4.27, p=0.002, 95% CI [8.10–27.10] (Figure 6b).
evidence: Statistical analysis of Rac1 inhibitor group showing preserved memory, with reference to Figure 6b.

claim: There was a significant difference in discrimination index between the saline and Rac1 inhibitor group, t(17) = 3.53, p=0.002, 95% CI [0.12–0.49].
source: There was a significant difference in discrimination index between the saline and Rac1 inhibitor group, t(17) = 3.53, p=0.002, 95% CI [0.12–0.49] (Figure 6c).
evidence: Statistical comparison of discrimination indices between saline and Rac1 inhibitor groups, with reference to Figure 6c.

claim: There was no difference in engram size between the saline and Rac1 inhibitor groups, t(10) = 1.09, p=0.29, 95% CI [–0.45 to 1.33].
source: Furthermore, there was no difference in engram size between the two groups, t(10) = 1.09, p=0.29, 95% CI [–0.45 to 1.33] (Figure 6d)
evidence: Statistical analysis showing no difference in engram size with Rac1 inhibition, with reference to Figure 6d.

claim: There was no difference in the level of neuronal activity within the dentate gyrus between saline and Rac1 inhibitor groups, t(10) = 0.86, p=0.40, 95% CI [–1.31 to 0.57].
source: or the level of neuronal activity within the dentate gyrus, t(10) = 0.86, p=0.40, 95% CI [–1.31 to 0.57] (Figure 6e).
evidence: Statistical analysis showing no difference in overall neuronal activity with Rac1 inhibition, with reference to Figure 6e.

claim: There was a significant decrease in engram reactivation between saline and Rac1 inhibitor groups, t(10) = 5.87, p<0.001, 95% CI [3.39–7.54].
source: However, there was a significant decrease in engram reactivation, t(10) = 5.87, p<0.001, 95% CI [3.39–7.54] (Figure 6f and g).
evidence: Statistical analysis showing significant difference in engram reactivation with Rac1 inhibition, with reference to Figure 6f and g.

claim: Control group mice spent more time exploring the novel object compared to the familiar object, suggesting intact memory recall, t(8) = 4.98, p=0.001, 95% CI [9.11–24.78].
source: During the object recall test, mice within the control group spent more time exploring the novel object compared to the familiar object, suggesting intact memory recall, t(8) = 4.98, p=0.001, 95% CI [9.11–24.78] (Figure 6i).
evidence: Statistical analysis of control group showing intact memory at 1 week, with reference to Figure 6i.

claim: Mice with Rac1 activator spent a similar amount of time exploring both the novel and familiar object, suggesting the original object memory was forgotten, t(7) = 1.19, p=0.27, 95% CI [–2.33 to 7.05].
source: Whereas mice with Rac1 activator spent a similar amount of time exploring both the novel and familiar object, suggesting the original object memory was forgotten, t(7) = 1.19, p=0.27, 95% CI [–2.33 to 7.05] (Figure 6i).
evidence: Statistical analysis of Rac1 activator group showing accelerated forgetting, with reference to Figure 6i.

claim: There was a significant difference between the discrimination index of the control and Rac1 activator group, t(15) = 3.68, p=0.002, 95% CI [–0.39 to –0.10].
source: There was a significant difference between the discrimination index of the control and Rac1 activator group, t(15) = 3.68, p=0.002, 95% CI [–0.39 to –0.10] (Figure 6j).
evidence: Statistical comparison of discrimination indices between control and Rac1 activator groups, with reference to Figure 6j.

claim: There was no difference in the engram size between control and Rac1 activator groups, t(12) = 0.29, p=0.77, 95% CI [–1.35 to 1.77].
source: Furthermore, there was no difference in the engram size, t(12) = 0.29, p=0.77, 95% CI [–1.35 to 1.77] (Figure 6k)
evidence: Statistical analysis showing no difference in engram size with Rac1 activation, with reference to Figure 6k.

claim: There was no difference in the level of neuronal activity within the dentate gyrus between control and Rac1 activator groups, t(12) = 0.23, p=0.81, 95% CI [–1.09 to 1.36].
source: or the level of neuronal activity within the dentate gyrus, t(12) = 0.23, p=0.81, 95% CI [–1.09 to 1.36] (Figure 6l).
evidence: Statistical analysis showing no difference in overall neuronal activity with Rac1 activation, with reference to Figure 6l.

claim: There was a decrease in engram reactivation with Rac1 activation, t(12) = 3.15, p=0.008, 95% CI [–13.98 to –2.56].
source: However, there was a decrease in engram reactivation, t(12) = 3.15, p=0.008, 95% CI [–13.98 to –2.56] (Figure 6m and n).
evidence: Statistical analysis showing decreased engram reactivation with Rac1 activation, with reference to Figure 6m and n.

claim: Rac1 signaling is involved in memory encoding and consolidation and may function as a plasticity enabling molecule to mediate retrievability.
source: Combined these data demonstrate the Rac1 signaling is involved in memory encoding and consolidation and may function as a plasticity enabling molecule to meditate retrievability.
evidence: Summary conclusion from Rac1 experiments proposing role of Rac1 in memory processes.

claim: Rac1 may be a signaling mechanism involved in adaptive forgetting.
source: Rac1 may therefore be a signaling mechanism involved in adaptive forgetting.
evidence: Speculative conclusion based on Rac1 experimental results.

claim: Forgetting is a dynamic process that can be explained as a gradient of engram activity, where the level of memory expression is experience-dependent and influenced by the animal's rate at which it learns from new experiences.
source: The data indicate that forgetting is a dynamic process that can be explained as a gradient of engram activity, where the level of memory expression is experience-dependent and influenced by the animal's rate at which it learns from new experiences.
evidence: Summary interpretation of all experimental findings proposing a model of forgetting.

claim: The Rescorla-Wagner model dynamically updates object-context associations in response to prediction errors.
source: Our proposed Rescorla-Wagner model dynamically updates object-context associations in response to prediction errors (Figure 7a).
evidence: Description of computational model used to explain experimental findings, with reference to Figure 7a.

claim: Engrams that are subjectively less relevant for adaptive behavior (representing weaker object-context associations) are more likely to be forgotten.
source: Accordingly, engrams that are subjectively less relevant for adaptive behavior (representing weaker object-context associations) are more likely to be forgotten (Todd and Holmes, 2022).
evidence: Key assumption of the computational model, supported by citation.

claim: Positive prediction errors strengthen the engram, and negative errors yield weaker object-context associations.
source: Positive prediction errors strengthen the engram, and negative errors yield weaker object-context associations (Figure 7d).
evidence: Mechanism of the computational model explaining how prediction errors affect engram strength, with reference to Figure 7d.

claim: Faster forgetting is driven by higher rates at which mice learn from negative prediction errors.
source: Therefore, faster forgetting is driven by higher rates at which mice learn from negative prediction errors.
evidence: Prediction of the computational model relating learning rate to forgetting speed.

claim: The animal predicts what it will encounter in its environment and adjusts these predictions as a function of its experiences.
source: The animal predicts what it will encounter in its environment (e.g. what objects) and adjusts these predictions as a function of its experiences (e.g. the presence or absence of objects).
evidence: Conceptual framework of the computational model describing predictive learning.

claim: Model simulations showed similar forgetting curves as mice in the experiment.
source: Supporting the idea that forgetting can be cast as an adaptive learning process, model simulations showed similar forgetting curves as mice in our experiment.
evidence: Comparison of computational model predictions to experimental data.

claim: The model fits the data better than a baseline model predicting random forgetting rates.
source: Finally, the model fits the data better than a baseline model predicting random forgetting rates, suggesting that it describes the data accurately and above chance level (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Model comparison analysis showing superior fit of Rescorla-Wagner model, with reference to Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Parameter-recovery analysis suggests that parameters can sufficiently be estimated despite the limited data for model fitting.
source: We also performed a parameter-recovery analysis suggesting that parameters can sufficiently be estimated despite the limited data for model fitting (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Validation analysis of computational model parameter estimation, with reference to Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Natural forgetting is a form of adaptive learning that alters engram accessibility in response to environmental feedback.
source: Our modeling results support the perspective that natural forgetting is a form of adaptive learning that alters engram accessibility in response to environmental feedback.
evidence: Summary conclusion from computational modeling supporting adaptive forgetting hypothesis.

claim: Environmental, optogenetic, and pharmacological manipulations might change the learning rate, suggesting that miscalibrated learning rates could give rise to pathological forgetting.
source: Accordingly, environmental, optogenetic, and pharmacological manipulations might change the learning rate, suggesting that miscalibrated learning rates could indeed give rise to pathological forgetting.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of modeling results relating learning rate to pathological conditions.

claim: Forgetting may be an adaptive form of engram plasticity which allows engrams to switch from an accessible state to an inaccessible state.
source: Together, these findings suggest that forgetting may be an adaptive form of engram plasticity which allows engrams to switch from an accessible state to an inaccessible state.
evidence: Main conclusion from abstract summarizing the overall findings of the study.

claim: Forgetting may function adaptively to improve learning and promote survival.
source: Forgetting, i.e., the loss of learned behavioral responses, may therefore function adaptively to improve learning and promote survival (Ryan and Frankland, 2022).
evidence: Theoretical statement about adaptive function of forgetting, supported by citation.

claim: Despite advancements in understanding the biology of engram cells, more work is still needed to fully elucidate how these cell ensembles contribute to the process of forgetting.
source: However, despite advancements in understanding the biology of engram cells, more work is still needed to fully elucidate how these cell ensembles contribute to the process of forgetting (Ryan and Frankland, 2022; Denny et al., 2017; Richards and Frankland, 2017).
evidence: Statement identifying gap in current knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Recent behavioral and physiological findings emphasize retrieval deficits as a key characteristic of memory impairment, supporting the idea that memory recall or accessibility may be driven by learning feedback from the environment.
source: We argue that a new conceptualization is necessitated by recent behavioral and physiological findings that emphasize retrieval deficits as a key characteristic of memory impairment, supporting the idea that memory recall or accessibility may be driven by learning feedback from the environment (Miller, 2021; Ryan and Frankland, 2022; Richards and Frankland, 2017; Perusini et al., 2017; Guskjolen et al., 2018; Roy et al., 2016; Autore et al., 2023).
evidence: Statement of current understanding in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Different forms of forgetting may exist along a gradient of engram activity or expression.
source: Recently it has been suggested that different forms of forgetting may exist along a gradient of engram activity or expression (Ryan and Frankland, 2022).
evidence: Theoretical framework from recent literature, supported by citation.

claim: Memory recall and forgetting require engram activity.
source: Indeed, numerous studies have suggested that memory recall (Perusini et al., 2017; Roy et al., 2016; Frankland et al., 2019; Josselyn and Frankland, 2018; Lei et al., 2022; Lv et al., 2019), and most recently forgetting, require engram activity (Autore et al., 2023; Khalaf et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement of findings from multiple studies, supported by citations.

claim: In other pathological and non-pathological states, forgetting may be due to reduced accessibility of engrams that otherwise endure.
source: However, in other pathological and non-pathological states, forgetting may be due to reduced accessibility of engrams that otherwise endure (McTighe et al., 2010).
evidence: Statement about alternative mechanism of forgetting, supported by citation.

claim: Altered engram accessibility may be caused by structural plasticity in the engram or by competing engrams of similar or recent experiences.
source: Altered engram accessibility may be caused by structural plasticity in the engram or indeed by competing engrams of similar or recent experiences (Ryan and Frankland, 2022; Autore et al., 2023; Davis and Zhong, 2017; Wang et al., 2020; Rao-Ruiz et al., 2019; Rashid et al., 2016; Poll et al., 2020).
evidence: Statement about potential mechanisms of altered engram accessibility, supported by citations.

claim: Natural forgetting represents a reversible suppression of engram ensembles due to experience and perceptual feedback, prompting cellular plasticity processes that modulate memory access adaptively.
source: We hypothesize that natural forgetting represents a reversible suppression of engram ensembles due to experience and perceptual feedback, prompting cellular plasticity processes that modulate memory access adaptively.
evidence: Main hypothesis of the study proposing mechanism of natural forgetting.

claim: The hippocampus is a fundamental structure for object memory.
source: In addition, they also support a role for the hippocampus as a fundamental structure for object memory (Cohen and Stackman, 2015; Cohen et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement about role of hippocampus in object memory, supported by citations.

claim: Forgetting may occur when an experience or an engram is not properly encoded during the learning phase, or not properly consolidated.
source: It is important to consider that forgetting may also occur when an experience or an engram is not properly encoded during the learning phase, or not properly consolidated (McGaugh, 2000; Dudai et al., 2015; Osorio-Gómez et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement about alternative causes of forgetting, supported by citations.

claim: The memory was properly consolidated 1 day post-training based on spine density observations.
source: In the present study forgetting was also associated with a reduction in spine density relative to a 24 hr recall time point. This observation suggested that the memory was properly consolidated 1 day post-training (Tonegawa et al., 2018).
evidence: Inference from spine density data suggesting proper consolidation, supported by citation.

claim: Intact memory recall at 1 week post-training supports the idea that the initial object memory was properly encoded and consolidated.
source: We also observed intact memory recall at 1 week post-training, which further supports the idea that the initial object memory was indeed properly encoded and consolidated.
evidence: Interpretation of behavioral data supporting proper encoding and consolidation.

claim: Forgetting may encompass a broad spectrum of types of memory loss, some involving actual loss of the engram, while others may reflect suppressed engram expression or altered conditions of engram activation.
source: Forgetting may encompass a broad spectrum of types of memory loss or apparent memory loss, some of which may involve the actual loss or damage of the engram, while others may reflect suppressed engram expression or simply altered conditions of engram activation.
evidence: Conceptual statement about different types of forgetting.

claim: The forgotten engram is still intact, as demonstrated by optogenetic reactivation triggering memory recall.
source: Our data showing memory retrieval following optogenetic reactivation demonstrate that the forgotten engram is indeed still intact, otherwise activation of those cells would no longer trigger memory recall.
evidence: Logical inference from optogenetic reactivation results about engram persistence.

claim: In amnesic states induced by protein synthesis inhibition or Alzheimer's disease, the engram remains intact even when memory consolidation is disrupted.
source: Interestingly, previous work has shown that an engram remains intact even when memory consolidation is disrupted by protein synthesis inhibition or transgenic induction of Alzheimer's disease (Perusini et al., 2017; Roy et al., 2016; Ryan et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement about engram persistence in pathological conditions, supported by citations.

claim: In amnesic states, the engram persists in a latent state despite lower dendritic spine density.
source: In those studies, the engram persists in a latent state despite lower dendritic spine density (Perusini et al., 2017; Roy et al., 2016; Ryan et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement about engram state in amnesia, supported by citations.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of amnesic engram cells was sufficient to restore access to the amnesic memory.
source: Moreover, optogenetic stimulation of amnesic engram cells was also sufficient to restore access to the amnesic memory (Perusini et al., 2017; Roy et al., 2016; Ryan et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement about optogenetic rescue of amnesic memories, supported by citations.

claim: The engram remains intact while not properly retrievable in amnesic states.
source: Taken together, these studies suggest the engram remains intact, while not properly retrievable (Perusini et al., 2017; Roy et al., 2016; Ryan et al., 2015).
evidence: Summary conclusion from cited studies about engram persistence and retrievability.

claim: Exposure to an enriched environment prior to learning improved engram reactivation and rescued memory recall in a mouse model of Fragile X syndrome.
source: These findings are supported by earlier work, which showed exposure to an enriched environment prior to learning improved engram reactivation and rescued memory recall in a mouse model of Fragile X syndrome (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: Statement about enrichment effects in disease model, supported by citation.

claim: Environmental enrichment alleviates pathological forms of memory impairment, such as Alzheimer's disease.
source: Previous literature has also shown the benefits of environmental enrichment in alleviating other pathological forms of memory impairment, such as Alzheimer's disease (Barak et al., 2013; Griñán-Ferré et al., 2018; Jankowsky et al., 2005).
evidence: Statement about enrichment effects in Alzheimer's disease, supported by citations.

claim: The effects of enrichment on learning and neural plasticity are well established and likely contribute to enhanced memory recall.
source: The effects of enrichment on learning and neural plasticity are well established and it is likely the contributing factor to the enhanced memory recall (Bekinschtein et al., 2011; Clemenson et al., 2015; O'Leary et al., 2019a; Griñán-Ferré et al., 2018; Epp et al., 2021; Snyder and Drew, 2020).
evidence: Statement about established effects of enrichment, supported by citations.

claim: The hippocampus has been identified as one of the only regions where postnatal neurogenesis continues throughout life.
source: The hippocampus has been identified as one of the only regions where postnatal neurogenesis continues throughout life (Snyder and Drew, 2020).
evidence: Statement of established fact about hippocampal neurogenesis, supported by citation.

claim: Levels of adult hippocampal neurogenesis can be altered by experience.
source: Levels of adult hippocampal neurogenesis do not remain constant and can be altered by experience (Clemenson et al., 2015; O'Leary et al., 2019a; O'Leary et al., 2019b; Denny et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement about experience-dependent neurogenesis, supported by citations.

claim: Adult-born neurons contribute to the process of forgetting.
source: In addition, adult-born neurons have also been shown to contribute to the process of forgetting (Epp et al., 2021; Frankland et al., 2013; Akers et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement about role of adult-born neurons in forgetting, supported by citations.

claim: The functional contribution of adult-born neurons to cognition and memory engrams is not fully understood.
source: Although the functional contribution of adult-born neurons to cognition and memory engrams is not fully understood (Ko and Frankland, 2021; Tran et al., 2022).
evidence: Statement identifying gap in knowledge about adult-born neurons, supported by citations.

claim: Immature neurons were actively recruited into the engram following a hippocampal-dependent task.
source: Mishra et al., 2022 showed that immature neurons were actively recruited into the engram following a hippocampal-dependent task.
evidence: Statement about findings from cited study on immature neuron recruitment.

claim: Increasing the level of neurogenesis rescued memory deficits by restoring engram activity in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease.
source: Increasing the level of neurogenesis rescued memory deficits by restoring engram activity, in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease (Mishra et al., 2022).
evidence: Statement about therapeutic effect of neurogenesis in disease model, supported by citation.

claim: Augmenting neurogenesis rescued deficits in spine density in both immature and mature engram neurons.
source: Specifically, augmenting neurogenesis rescued the deficits in spine density in both immature and mature engram neurons (Mishra et al., 2022).
evidence: Statement about morphological effects of neurogenesis manipulation, supported by citation.

claim: Forgetting could be reversed following a brief reminder experience, which was associated with a corresponding increase in engram activity.
source: Our results showed that forgetting could be reversed following a brief reminder experience, which was associated with a corresponding increase in engram activity.
evidence: Summary of reminder experiment results showing reversal of forgetting.

claim: Contextual changes from the passage of time can lead to retrieval failure.
source: In fact, earlier work by Bouton and colleagues has demonstrated that contextual changes from the passage of time can lead to retrieval failure (Bouton, 1993; Bouton et al., 1999; Rosas and Bouton, 1997).
evidence: Statement about context-dependent memory retrieval, supported by citations.

claim: The degree of learning and memory specificity corresponded with engram activity.
source: Our findings indicate that the degree of learning and memory specificity corresponded with engram activity (Leake et al., 2021).
evidence: Summary statement about relationship between learning specificity and engram activity, supported by citation.

claim: The learning rate was altered following environmental enrichment and repeated context exposure, which affected the rate of forgetting.
source: Here, the learning rate was altered following environmental enrichment as well as following repeated context exposure, which in turn affected the rate of forgetting.
evidence: Summary of computational modeling results showing learning rate changes with different manipulations.

claim: There may be an 'optimal' learning rate that yields environmentally adaptive, natural forgetting.
source: Together, this suggests the possibility of an 'optimal' learning rate that yields environmentally adaptive, natural forgetting and that learning rates that are too high may be linked to amnesia and learning rates that are too low to some sort of hypermnesia.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of modeling results proposing optimal learning rate concept.

claim: Learning rates that are too high may be linked to amnesia and learning rates that are too low to hypermnesia.
source: Together, this suggests the possibility of an 'optimal' learning rate that yields environmentally adaptive, natural forgetting and that learning rates that are too high may be linked to amnesia and learning rates that are too low to some sort of hypermnesia.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis about pathological learning rates.

claim: A lack of memory expression would constitute forgetting due to the loss of learned behavioral response in the presence of natural retrieval cues.
source: Within our behavioral paradigm, a lack of memory expression would still constitute forgetting due to the loss of learned behavioral response in the presence of natural retrieval cues.
evidence: Conceptual definition of forgetting within the study's framework.

claim: Changes in memory expression may underlie the adaptive nature of forgetting.
source: The changes in memory expression may therefore underlie the adaptive nature of forgetting.
evidence: Interpretive statement connecting memory expression changes to adaptive forgetting.

claim: The Rescorla-Wagner model can be used to describe forgetting as a process of learning, where experience alters the degree of association between retrieval cues and memory.
source: The Rescorla-Wagner model can be used to describe forgetting as a process of learning, where experience alters the degree of association between retrieval cues and memory (Todd and Holmes, 2022; Yau and McNally, 2023).
evidence: Statement about application of Rescorla-Wagner model to forgetting, supported by citations.

claim: Memories more relevant for adaptive behavior are more likely to be accessible than memories representing irrelevant, outdated information.
source: Based upon this idea, we proposed a parsimonious computational model that integrates our findings into a cognitively plausible framework in which memories more relevant for adaptive behavior are more likely to be accessible than memories representing irrelevant, outdated information.
evidence: Key principle of the computational model relating memory relevance to accessibility.

claim: An emergent property underlying forgetting is the prediction error.
source: This model suggests that an emergent property underlying forgetting is the prediction error.
evidence: Key insight from computational model about role of prediction error.

claim: Forgetting is a form of learning whereby experience drives changes in the learning rate of an organism, and the expectation of one's environment can alter the efficiency of recall through forgetting plasticity.
source: Within this framework, forgetting is a form of learning whereby experience drives changes in the learning rate of an organism, and the expectation of one's environment can alter the efficiency of recall through forgetting plasticity (Ryan and Frankland, 2022).
evidence: Conceptual framework statement about forgetting as learning, supported by citation.

claim: Prediction errors may determine whether an engram is strengthened or weakened.
source: It therefore follows that prediction errors may determine whether an engram is strengthened, leading to higher engram expression, or weakened, leading to lower engram expression (Figure 7d).
evidence: Mechanistic prediction from computational model about prediction error effects, with reference to Figure 7d.

claim: Positive prediction errors indicate that an unexpected event has taken place and induce plasticity processes that increase the likelihood of engram expression.
source: Positive prediction errors indicate that an unexpected event has taken place (e.g. some unexpected object is present). We assume that positive errors induce plasticity processes that alter the engram and increase the likelihood of engram expression.
evidence: Mechanistic explanation from computational model about positive prediction errors.

claim: Negative prediction errors indicate that something expected has not taken place and induce forgetting plasticity yielding decreased engram expression.
source: In contrast, negative errors indicate that something that was expected has not taken place (e.g. object absent). Consequently, negative errors induce forgetting plasticity and yield decreased engram expression.
evidence: Mechanistic explanation from computational model about negative prediction errors.

claim: Dopamine is known to play a role in prediction error and learning rates.
source: Dopamine is known to play a role in prediction error and learning rates (Cai et al., 2020; Kalisch et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement about dopamine's role in learning, supported by citations.

claim: Dopamine has been shown to differently regulate Rac1 to modulate behavioral plasticity.
source: Moreover, dopamine has been shown to differently regulate Rac1 to modulate behavioral plasticity (Davis and Zhong, 2017; Tu et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement about dopamine-Rac1 interaction, supported by citations.

claim: Rac1 impairs memory recall by driving forgetting-induced plasticity.
source: This finding is in agreement with previous work where Rac1 impaired memory recall by driving forgetting-induced plasticity (Davis and Zhong, 2017; Liu et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2016; Shuai et al., 2010; Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement about Rac1's role in forgetting, supported by citations.

claim: Rac1 functions during the memory encoding and consolidation phases and contributes to active forgetting.
source: Rac1 has been shown to function during the memory encoding and consolidation phases, and thereby to contribute to active forgetting (Davis and Zhong, 2017; Liu et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2016; Shuai et al., 2010; Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2020).
evidence: Statement about Rac1's role in memory phases, supported by citations.

claim: A social reward enabled latent engrams to switch to active engrams via suppression of Rac1 activity in CA1 neurons of the hippocampus.
source: Lei et al., 2022 demonstrated that a social reward enabled latent engrams to switch to active engrams via suppression of Rac1 activity in CA1 neurons of the hippocampus.
evidence: Statement about findings from cited study on social reward and Rac1.

claim: Social stress switched active memory engrams back to latent engrams through activation of Rac1 signaling.
source: It was further demonstrated that this effect was bidirectional as a social stressor switched active memory engrams back to latent engrams (Lei et al., 2022). This social stress-induced forgetting was modulated through the activation of Rac1 signaling (Lei et al., 2022).
evidence: Statement about findings from cited study on social stress and Rac1.

claim: The activation of Rac1 accelerates the rate of forgetting, while its inhibition prevents forgetting.
source: Overall, the activation of Rac1 has been shown to accelerate the rate of forgetting, while its inhibition prevented forgetting (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: Summary statement about Rac1's bidirectional effects on forgetting, supported by citation.

claim: Rac1-induced changes in memory recall alter engram reactivation.
source: Here, our work advanced this knowledge by demonstrating that Rac1-induced changes in memory recall alter engram reactivation.
evidence: Statement about novel contribution of current study regarding Rac1 and engram reactivation.

claim: Rac1 is involved in altering the rate of forgetting at multiple time intervals after learning, not just immediately after learning.
source: These works support our data suggesting that Rac1 is involved in altering the rate of forgetting at multiple time intervals after learning, not just immediately after learning.
evidence: Interpretation of current and previous findings about temporal scope of Rac1's effects.

claim: Rac1 may function like a ubiquitous plasticity enabling molecule that is involved in memory encoding, consolidation, forgetting, and retrieval, depending on the experimental conditions and behavioral settings.
source: Our broader view is that Rac1 may function like a ubiquitous plasticity enabling molecule that is involved in memory encoding, consolidation, forgetting, and retrieval, depending on the experimental conditions and behavioral settings (Ryan and Frankland, 2022; Davis and Zhong, 2017).
evidence: Broad interpretive statement about Rac1's multifaceted role in memory, supported by citations.

claim: Retroactive interference emerges from the interplay of multiple engrams competing for expression.
source: Recent work suggests that retroactive interference emerges from the interplay of multiple engrams competing for expression (Autore et al., 2023).
evidence: Statement about mechanism of interference, supported by citation.

claim: Extinction training suppressed the reactivation of a fear engram, while activating a second putative extinction ensemble.
source: Lacagnina et al., 2019 demonstrated that extinction training suppressed the reactivation of a fear engram, while activating a second putative extinction ensemble.
evidence: Statement about findings from cited study on extinction and engrams.

claim: Extinction engram cells and reward cells were shown to be functionally interchangeable.
source: In another study, these extinction engram cells and reward cells were shown to be functionally interchangeable (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: Statement about findings from cited study on engram cell function.

claim: The balance between extinction and acquisition was disrupted by inhibiting the extinction recruited neurons in the central nucleus of the amygdala.
source: Moreover, in a study conducted by Lay et al., 2023, the balance between extinction and acquisition was disrupted by inhibiting the extinction recruited neurons in the central nucleus of the amygdala.
evidence: Statement about findings from cited study on extinction mechanisms.

claim: Decision making after extinction was governed by a balance between acquisition and extinction-specific ensembles.
source: These results suggested that decision making after extinction was governed by a balance between acquisition and extinction-specific ensembles (Lay et al., 2023).
evidence: Statement about findings from cited study on decision making and engrams.

claim: Having access to a large number of memories is adaptive in vast environments, but it is equally important to prioritize the accessibility of the most relevant memories and to forget outdated information.
source: While having access to a large number of memories is adaptive in vast environments, it is equally important to prioritize the accessibility of the most relevant memories and to forget outdated information.
evidence: Conceptual statement about adaptive value of selective memory accessibility.

claim: Suppressing stored information through natural forgetting might promote adaptive behavior.
source: Suppressing stored information through natural forgetting might therefore promote adaptive behavior.
evidence: Conceptual statement about adaptive function of forgetting.

claim: Forgetting too much (amnesia) or too little (hypermnesia) under pathological conditions is maladaptive.
source: However, forgetting too much (e.g. amnesia) or too little (hypermnesia) under pathological conditions is maladaptive.
evidence: Statement about pathological extremes of forgetting.

claim: Natural forgetting may be considered a form of adaptive learning where engrams that are subjectively less relevant for behavior are more likely to be forgotten.
source: Based on these findings and our computational model in which memories subjectively less relevant to adaptive behavior are more likely to be forgotten, we conclude that natural forgetting may be considered a form of adaptive learning where engrams that are subjectively less relevant for behavior are more likely to be forgotten.
evidence: Main conclusion of the study integrating experimental and computational findings.
